transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-11
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 min
Attendees: Jordan Reed (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (Aegis CTO), Priya Kapoor (Aegis ML Eng), Liam O'Neill (Aegis SRE)

Summary: Quick discovery to understand Aegis's latency & context requirements, multilingual coverage, and whether Hosted, Dedicated, or Private (on-prem/VPC) makes sense. Customer cares about 32k+ context, Spanish/Portuguese + simplified Chinese, retrieval/tool-calling for live inventory APIs, and strict audit/KMS needs. We agreed to run a small perf pilot and share security artifacts.

Topics: context length requirements, open-model tradeoffs, multilingual quality, tool calling/function-calls, VPC/on-prem constraints, SOC2/KMS, pilot logistics

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Reed: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Maya Chen our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Tom Alvarez: Hey Jordan, good — thanks. We've got a hard stop at 4:50, so try to keep it tight. I'm Tom, CTO. Priya and Liam are with me.
[00:18] Priya Kapoor: Hi, yeah, thanks.
[00:20] Liam O'Neill: Morning, all.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Great. Quick agenda: understand your current stack, numbers (qps, latency SLOs), the model/quality requirements especially for multilingual, and deployment constraints — e.g., do you need on-prem or is VPC enough. Then we can map Hosted/Dedicated/Private options and propose a pilot. Sound good?
[00:36] Tom Alvarez: Yep, that's perfect. To start, our core use case is a conversational assistant embedded in our enterprise portal for internal ops and customer-facing guides. Typical session is 6–10 turns, but we also have batch jobs that summarize long incident logs — some logs run 60k tokens. So context is a big deal.
[00:50] Jordan Reed: Got it, so two main patterns: interactive chat with medium context and long-form RAG/summarization for very long docs. What's your SLO on latency for the interactive flow?
[00:58] Priya Kapoor: For agent-style chat, ideally under 400–500ms p50 for short prompts; p95 can be a bit higher but we need predictability. For the long summarization jobs we expect higher latency but want reasonable throughput.
[01:12] Maya Chen: Okay — that's doable, but tradeoffs become important. If you run large-context models (32k–64k) you pay more in latency/cost; Dedicated with pinning and optimized kernels helps. Also prefix KV caching helps improve latency for multi-turn sessions.
[01:28] Liam O'Neill: When you say KV cache does Redwood do prefix caching across sessions or per-instance? What's the cache invalidation policy?
[01:36] Maya Chen: Good q — we do per-model prefix and KV cache with configurable TTLs. For Hosted we provide managed caching; Dedicated gives you more control and we can expose hooks for purge on deploys. In some private setups customers want local LRU caches, which we support in the on-prem package. Note: the transcript engine occasionally transcribed that as KVC ache earlier — apologies, ums.
[01:55] Tom Alvarez: Ha, noted. On models — we're evaluating open models. The team has seen Mistral, Llama2 variants, and some of the newer Red-verified candidates. Our main concerns: multilingual quality in Spanish/Portuguese/Chinese and tool-calling reliability when we hit enterprise APIs. Thoughts?
[02:12] Maya Chen: From a quality standpoint, Mistral variants are strong for English and some European languages, but Chinese quality varies. Llama2-13B- or 70B with instruction tuning can be good, and some 30B trajectories that Redwood-verified show solid throughput. For tool calling — function calls (we support OpenAI-style function calling) are available across models but latency/serialization differs. For high throughput tool calling we recommend Dedicated so you avoid noisy neighbor effects.
[02:36] Priya Kapoor: Do you support multi-model routing? Say we prefer a cheaper 7B on most queries and a 30B for higher-risk or longer-context queries.
[02:44] Jordan Reed: Yes — smart routing is a core feature. You can route by intent, token length, latency target, or price. For example, short queries to 7B for cost, and long or hallucination-prone queries to the 30B ver. We even support automatic fallback to a lower-cost model if capacity is constrained, or the opposite if quality degrades.
[03:02] Liam O'Neill: Network and security — is there an option to do a private control plane with VPC peering? We can't send some of our logs to public hosting.
[03:10] Maya Chen: Absolutely. Redwood Private provides a customer-managed control plane in your VPC; we can also do an on-prem deployment for air-gapped environments. For most customers VPC + KMS integration (we support customer-managed KMS/HSM) is sufficient. We also have audit logs exported to your SIEM.
[03:27] Tom Alvarez: SOC2 and ISO — do you have those? We need auditors' contact and evidence for our procurement process.
[03:32] Jordan Reed: Yes, SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 — we'll share the certs and our compliance pack after the call. I'll include the security whitepaper and the on-prem packaging notes.
[03:42] Priya Kapoor: Back to models — Priya: you mentioned quantization earlier. If we quantize Llama2/13B to int8 or int4, what's the expected drop in multilingual quality? We're particularly anxious about Chinese with int4.
[03:54] Maya Chen: Good question. Int8 is usually safe with negligible drop for many languages. Int4 is more aggressive — some models maintain quality well, others degrade, especially for non-Latin scripts. For Chinese we'd generally recommend int8 or mixed-precision pipelines and to validate with a small eval. That's why we'll run the bench for you including multilingual prompts.
[04:12] Tom Alvarez: Great. About context: you mentioned 32k and 64k — our logs hit 60k tokens — is 64k supported and what are the performance implications?
[04:21] Maya Chen: We have models and runtime paths that support 64k contexts. Throughput for 64k is lower and memory footprint increases; kernel selection and sequence chunking matter. For heavy summarization we often recommend a pre-chunking RAG layer: run an embed + search to find most relevant passages (reduce to say 12k tokens) before final compression summary. But if you need full 60k context in a single generation, that's possible on Dedicated or Private with tuned kernels.
[04:44] Liam O'Neill: If we go Dedicated, what's the onboarding? Do you provision a pool? What's autoscaling look like?
[04:50] Jordan Reed: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools configured to your throughput. You get predictable qps and can set autoscale policies and burst capacity. Onboarding typically 2–4 weeks: provisioning, model onboarding, private keys, and testing. For pilots we often do a small reserved pool for two weeks.
[05:04] Tom Alvarez: Pricing — is there a per-token price plus a reserved capacity cost? We'd like to see a matrix showing expected monthly costs at different qps.
[05:10] Jordan Reed: Yes, Hosted is usage-based per-token. Dedicated combines reserved monthly capacity plus lower per-token execution costs and optional burst rates. We'll send a pricing spreadsheet that models your expected qps and mixes of model sizes.
[05:21] Priya Kapoor: For tool calling — we need robust retries and idempotency when calling our inventory and billing APIS. Can Redwood handle structured tools with guaranteed delivery semantics?
[05:30] Maya Chen: We surface function-calling with structured JSON outputs and have retry/backoff patterns. Guaranteed delivery semantics for external APIs typically sit in your gateway but we can add a persistence/queueing shim in the flow on Dedicated or Private. We'll put an architecture note in the follow-up.
[05:44] Tom Alvarez: Any known vendors we should watch for compatibility issues? We use an internal vector DB but might use Pinecone for testing.
[05:51] Maya Chen: We integrate with common vector DBs (Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate) and can adapt to internal vector stores via connectors. If you share the vector API we can test connectivity in the pilot.
[06:02] Liam O'Neill: One operational question: token-level cost visibility. Can we see per-route, per-token breakdown in the console? We need cost attribution to teams.
[06:10] Jordan Reed: Yes — Redwood Console has per-route/model token breakdown, trace hooks, and cost attribution at token level. You can export reports or connect to BI.
[06:18] Priya Kapoor: For the perf bench you mentioned: can you run our dataset with our prompt templates and our evaluation metrics?
[06:24] Maya Chen: Yes — if you share redacted samples and the prompt templates we'll run them across the 3 candidate models with your metrics (accuracy / F1 for QA, Rouge for summarization, and latency p50/p95). We'll include both Hosted emulation and Dedicated tuned runs.
[06:38] Tom Alvarez: Ok that sounds good. Anything else on compliance? We might need data residency in EU for a subset.
[06:44] Jordan Reed: We have EU regions and can pin data to region. For stricter residency we can discuss Private deployments with a customer-controlled region.
[06:52] Priya Kapoor: Small nit: function calling for multi-turn — if the model invokes tools mid-conversation and we rely on the tool to augment context, will Redwood handle KV cache updates so the next model call sees the updated state?
[07:03] Maya Chen: Yes, we support KV cache writes triggered by tool results; you can flush or persist them depending on your policy. That is easier on Dedicated/Private where you can control cache TTL and storage. We'll show a sample flow in the follow-up.
[07:18] Jordan Reed: Great. Quick recap and concrete next steps?
[07:22] Tom Alvarez: Please send SOC2/ISO and the on-prem pack. We'll provide sample logs and prompts. We want the perf bench results and a pricing sheet. Also let's pencil in Jan 10–24 for a Dedicated pilot — subject to final sign-off.
[07:34] Jordan Reed: Will do. Action items we've captured: security pack and pricing from me by Dec 15; Maya to run bench and share spreadsheet by Dec 20; Aegis to send redacted samples by Dec 14; Liam to confirm network topology by Dec 18.
[07:46] Priya Kapoor: Sounds good — thanks all.
[07:48] Liam O'Neill: Thanks, bye.
[07:49] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone.
[07:50] Jordan Reed: Thanks! We'll follow up with calendar invite and the docs.

Notes on transcript quality: some technical terms transcribed imperfectly (K V cache -> KVC ache, Mistral sometimes as "mister all"). Speaker turns occasionally overlap.

References shared during call: Redwood security pack (link to be sent), pricing matrix (to be sent), perf bench template (Redwood SE doc link), pilot calendar invite (to be scheduled).
